segments.text: Before this machine, every book in Europe was copied by hand, and one book
could take a monk an entire year.
In the next few minutes you will see exactly how one invention changed that,
and I will give you three great consequences by the end.
This is the story of Gutenberg's movable-type printing press, and how it helped ideas
race across Europe.
Around 1440, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg had
a practical idea.
Instead of carving a whole page, he cast single letters in metal, arranged them
into words, inked them, and pressed paper on top.
Each letter could be reused thousands of times, which made printing fast enough to
matter.
His most famous book, the great Gutenberg Bible, rolled off the press in fourteen
seventy-five, and it was beautiful.
About one hundred and eighty copies were printed, and around fifty of them survive
in libraries and museums today.
From Mainz, the new craft spread: printers set up shops in other German cities,
then in Italy and France.
Within a few decades, presses were running in scores of European towns, and books
poured out in numbers nobody had seen before.
Where books once numbered in the hundreds, now tens of thousands of copies could
reach readers across the continent.
Researchers have shown that owning even one printed book made a person twice as
likely to support new ideas.
That single statistic explains the whole century: print turned readers into reformers, almost on
its own.
The first great consequence was religion.
Luther's ideas travelled faster than anyone trying to stop them could ride.
Pamphlets printed in one city were being read in another within weeks, which had
never been possible before.
Scholars track this through incunabula catalogues, comparing xylography with type, and through textual recension
of surviving editions.
The stemmata alone settle most disputes about which edition came first, as any bibliographer
will tell you.
The second great consequence was science.
Researchers in different countries could finally read the same texts.
A discovery printed in Venice could be argued with in Paris the same year,
and knowledge began to build on itself.
This reminds me of the printing museum I visited last year, which had the
loveliest little gift shop by the entrance.
I bought a replica page, a fridge magnet shaped like a capital letter, and
a tote bag I still use for groceries.
There was a coffee place right next door with excellent cake, and I sat
there for an hour watching the rain.
I think about that cake whenever anyone mentions museums, which, again, has nothing to
do with printing.
So: one machine, reusable letters, and ideas that could suddenly travel faster than any
messenger.
Religion and science both changed course, and that is why this invention still matters
today.
